name: Globe and Mail cryptic crossword No 3,138

clue.text: Island in March — a heavenly place

indicators.note: one thing sitting in another means it is placed inside it

blocks.note: to march is to parade; here read as a noun, a parade
IS is the standard abbreviation for island

explanation.surface: A travel blurb: an island visited in March is paradise.
explanation.walkthrough: The capital on 'March' makes it look like the month, but it is the verb or noun for walking in step.
explanation.definitionFit: Paradise is heaven itself, and by extension any blissful spot, so it is a fitting synonym.

clue.text: Urge American to visit public house

indicators.note: a visitor goes inside the place visited, so one piece enters another

blocks.note: PH is the map abbreviation for a public house
US is short for American

explanation.surface: Someone urges an American tourist to try a pub.
explanation.walkthrough: A public house is a British pub; PH marks one on maps.
explanation.definitionFit: To push someone is to press or encourage them strongly, the same as urging them.

clue.text: Unusual coin that’s plated

definitions.note: a descriptive phrase standing for a noun: something served on a plate

blocks.note: rare means unusual
a bit is an old coin, as in the British threepenny bit or the American two bits

explanation.surface: A collector's odd coin turns out to be merely plated, not solid metal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plated' suggests a coin with a thin metal coating; the setter means served on a plate. Welsh rarebit is cheese sauce on toast.
explanation.definitionFit: Rarebit is a dish, melted cheese on toast, so it is a thing that gets served up on a plate.

clue.text: Bandaged own toe, Arthur? To some extent that’s practical

indicators.note: only part of the run of words is wanted, so the answer sits partly within them

blocks.note: the letters run from the end of the first word to the middle of the last

explanation.surface: Arthur bandaging his own injured toe is a sensible, practical act.
explanation.walkthrough: The run begins with the final D of 'Bandaged' and stops partway through 'Arthur'.
explanation.definitionFit: A down-to-earth person is sensible and realistic, the idiomatic equivalent of practical in outlook.

clue.text: Provide drink Polly regularly downed

indicators.note: at regular intervals means every other letter is kept

blocks.note: to sup is to drink, or a sip
first, third and fifth letters

explanation.surface: Polly knocks back a drink provided for her.
explanation.walkthrough: 'downed' does no work beyond the surface image of Polly drinking; in this down clue it simply has the drink placed above her letters.
explanation.definitionFit: To supply goods or help is to provide them; the two verbs are straightforward synonyms.

clue.text: Missing second item for auction houses

indicators.note: to house something is to give it shelter inside

blocks.note: each item sold at an auction is a lot
S is the abbreviation for second

explanation.surface: An auction catalogue notes a missing second item, as if auction houses lost it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'auction houses' reads as one noun, the saleroom firms; split it so 'houses' is a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: Something lost cannot be found, which is exactly what missing means.

clue.text: Hold forth over cost

blocks.note: O is the cricket scoring abbreviation for an over
a rate is a price or charge

explanation.surface: Someone lectures at length about a price.
explanation.walkthrough: 'over' looks like 'about', but here it is the cricket over: a set of six balls bowled, written O on scorecards.
explanation.definitionFit: To orate is to deliver a long pompous speech, the same as holding forth to listeners.

clue.text: Redesign seediest area in the north

indicators.note: a redesign lays things out again in a new arrangement

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A planner proposes regenerating the shabbiest district up north.
explanation.walkthrough: Teesside is the industrial region around the River Tees, including Middlesbrough, in northeast England.
explanation.definitionFit: Teesside is a named region of northeast England, so it is an example of a northern area.

clue.text: Old show featuring Queen Kate, notoriously

indicators.note: to feature something is to include it, so one piece goes inside another

blocks.note: shew is the archaic spelling of show
R stands for Regina, Latin for queen

explanation.surface: A vintage TV programme starring the Queen and Kate, a royal scandal.
explanation.walkthrough: Kate looks like the Princess of Wales beside a queen; she is Katherine of Shakespeare's The Taming of the Shrew.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare's Kate is the title character of The Taming of the Shrew, famous as a bad-tempered, scolding woman.

clue.text: Dad left each locale after draining beer

indicators.note: to drain something is to empty its contents, leaving only the outside

blocks.note: pa is an informal word for father
L is the abbreviation for left
EA is the abbreviation for each
first and last letters only

explanation.surface: Dad walks out of every pub once he has finished his drink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'draining beer' paints Dad finishing a pint, but 'draining' acts on 'locale', and 'beer' stands alone as the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Pale ale is a type of light-coloured, hop-forward bitter, so it is a specific kind of beer.

clue.text: Where Hollywood is cold about musical classic film

indicators.note: about can mean around in a jumble, so the letters are scattered and reset

blocks.note: Hollywood is a district of Los Angeles
taken as written
Evita is the Lloyd Webber musical about Eva Perón

explanation.surface: Hollywood, chilly towards a famous movie musical.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' looks like a container signal, but it rearranges the four letters of the word before it.
explanation.definitionFit: La Dolce Vita is Fellini's celebrated 1960 Italian movie, widely ranked among cinema's greatest classics.

clue.text: Jesse stripped off, having first fought Resistance in uniform

indicators.note: stripping peels away the outer layer, so the edges go and the middle stays
one piece is put at the front of the others, ahead of the rest

blocks.note: to battle is to fight
R is the symbol for electrical resistance
the name without its first and last letters

explanation.surface: Jesse strips to fight the Resistance, wearing his uniform: a wartime scene.
explanation.walkthrough: 'stripped off' suggests undressing, but it trims the name's outer letters; 'having first' puts the fighting before the rest.
explanation.definitionFit: Battledress is the everyday combat uniform worn by soldiers, so it is a kind of uniform.

clue.text: Musical morning in Paris?

indicators.note: one thing in another is placed inside it

blocks.note: Paris Hilton, the celebrity heiress; the question mark flags the name trick
AM is the abbreviation for morning

explanation.surface: A song about a French morning, perhaps from a stage show.
explanation.walkthrough: 'morning in Paris' wants to be MATIN; Paris is a first name, and her surname takes the morning inside.
explanation.definitionFit: Hamilton is Lin-Manuel Miranda's hit hip-hop stage show about the American founding father.

clue.text: Learnt about feature of browser?

indicators.note: about can mean all around, in disorder, so the letters are moved

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone discovered a feature of their web browser.
explanation.walkthrough: 'browser' looks like Chrome or Firefox; it is an animal that browses, nibbling leaves and shoots, such as a deer.
explanation.definitionFit: Deer feed by browsing on shrubs, and their most distinctive physical feature is the branching horn on the head.

clue.text: Charlie wearing tartan, looking cool

indicators.note: a wearer is inside the clothes worn, so one piece is wrapped by another

blocks.note: plaid is tartan cloth
Charlie is C in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: Charlie strolls about in a tartan outfit, looking stylish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cool' suggests fashionable, which suits the tartan picture; here it means calm and unruffled.
explanation.definitionFit: A placid person appears calm and unflustered, which is what looking cool, as in composed, conveys.

clue.text: Man from Barcelona possibly upset Arsenal at a corner somewhat

indicators.note: somewhat means to a degree, so only part of the words is used
upset means overturned, so in a down clue the letters read bottom to top

blocks.note: the run spans the end of the first word to the start of the last

explanation.surface: A Barcelona player perhaps beat Arsenal from a corner kick.
explanation.walkthrough: Arsenal is a London football club; the football surface hides the letters running backwards through the phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: Barcelona is the capital of Catalonia, so a native of the city is, by example, a Catalonian.

clue.text: Hollow, faint pulse periodically taken

indicators.note: taken at intervals means every other letter is kept

blocks.note: dim means faint or weak
first, third and fifth letters

explanation.surface: A nurse checks a weak, empty-feeling pulse at intervals.
explanation.walkthrough: 'periodically taken' sounds like a nurse taking a pulse every so often; it keeps alternate letters of the word.
explanation.definitionFit: A dimple is a small natural dent in the skin or a surface, a little hollow.

clue.text: I met Pinter, roughly around November … so rude!

indicators.note: roughly means not precisely, so the letters come out in a loose order
around means surrounding, so one piece sits within another

blocks.note: taken as written
November is N in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: Someone recalls a brusque encounter with playwright Harold Pinter late one autumn.
explanation.walkthrough: 'roughly around November' reads as a date; it splits into a mixing signal and a containing one.
explanation.definitionFit: Impertinent means disrespectfully cheeky, a stronger synonym for being rude to someone.

clue.text: New moon possibly to disturb, by the sound of it

indicators.note: the answer is judged by how it is heard, not how it is spelt

blocks.note: to faze is to disturb or unsettle

explanation.surface: A new moon, some say, can unsettle people.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is an example, flagged by 'possibly'.
explanation.definitionFit: The new moon is one stage in the lunar cycle, alongside crescent, quarter and full, each called by that name.

clue.text: Deserted area leaving Dodge

indicators.note: something leaving departs, so it is taken out

blocks.note: to dodge is to avoid
A is the abbreviation for area

explanation.surface: A Wild West scene: everyone has left Dodge City, now a ghost town.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dodge' with its capital looks like the town; it is the verb to dodge.
explanation.definitionFit: A void is empty, without occupants, the same sense as an abandoned, deserted place.

clue.text: A pot she stirred here?

indicators.note: stirring mixes things up, so the letters get churned into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Where might a woman have been stirring a pot?
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue defines the place: a waitress stirring a pot of tea would be in one.
explanation.definitionFit: A tea shop is a café serving pots of tea, just where a server might stir one.

clue.text: US soldier going over facilities in White House

indicators.note: going over means turning over, so the letters run backwards

blocks.note: GI is slang for an American soldier
the facilities is a polite word for a toilet; loo is British for toilet

explanation.surface: An American soldier checks the bathrooms in the President's residence.
explanation.walkthrough: 'White House' plainly wants the President's home; read literally it is a house made of white snow.
explanation.definitionFit: An igloo is an Inuit dome built of snow blocks, literally a dwelling that is white.

clue.text: Christmas verse taken from A Christmas Carol?

indicators.note: taken from means removed out of, so a letter is subtracted

blocks.note: Dickens's A Christmas Carol is a short novel; the question mark admits it is an example
V is the abbreviation for verse

explanation.surface: A seasonal poem quoted from Dickens's festive story.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Christmas verse' reads as one phrase, a carol; split it, so the first word defines and 'verse' is the letter to remove.
explanation.definitionFit: Noel is a word for the festive season, borrowed from French Noël, used on cards and in carols.

clue.text: Won back Georgia having exercised restraint externally

indicators.note: externally means on the outside, so one piece wraps around the other

blocks.note: to rein is to restrain, as with a horse's reins
GA is the US state abbreviation for Georgia

explanation.surface: A politician recaptures Georgia by campaigning with restraint.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Won back Georgia' reads as one election story; 'Won back' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To regain something is to recover possession of it after losing it, like recapturing a prize.
